adjudication.notes: Cross-stakeholder contradiction between Mr. Davis and Dr. Chen over lab period block structure.

episodes.topic: Master timetable constraints and faculty instructional loads
Science lab facilities and consecutive double-block contradiction
Teacher classroom mobility anti-goal and missing student stakeholders
Biometric attendance rejection and school community harmony

goals.statement: The master schedule allocates student course enrollments without room collisions or instructor double-bookings.

grounding.quote: The scheduling system must allocate student course enrollments without room collisions or teacher double-bookings.

acceptable_paraphrases: Assign course sections avoiding teacher and classroom schedule overlaps.

goals.statement: Full-time teaching staff do not exceed five instructional periods per instructional day.

grounding.quote: Full-time teaching staff should not exceed five instructional periods per day to ensure sufficient grading and lesson preparation time.

acceptable_paraphrases: Cap faculty teaching load at five periods daily.

goals.statement: Advanced science laboratory courses are scheduled in consecutive double periods on the same instructional day.

grounding.quote: Advanced biology and chemistry laboratories must always be scheduled in consecutive double periods on the same day so experiments finish properly.

acceptable_paraphrases: Block science labs into paired consecutive periods.

goals.statement: Laboratory periods are distributed across alternate days to protect humanities elective scheduling.

grounding.quote: Consecutive double periods destroy split-period humanities scheduling across elective blocks, so lab periods must remain split across alternate days.

acceptable_paraphrases: Split lab sessions across non-consecutive days to preserve humanities offerings.

goals.statement: The timetable avoids scheduling junior faculty to more than three distinct classroom room relocations per day.

grounding.quote: The timetable must never schedule junior teachers to more than three distinct classroom relocations in a single instructional day, because carting teaching materials across campus exhausts them.

acceptable_paraphrases: Do not assign junior teachers more than three room changes on any single day.

goals.statement: The scheduling algorithm maximizes student placement into their preferred elective courses.

grounding.quote: The scheduling algorithm should maximize placement of students into their top-choice elective courses.

acceptable_paraphrases: Optimize student placement rates into requested elective courses.

goals.statement: The school community experiences an orderly, conflict-free transition into the new academic year.

grounding.quote: A calm, conflict-free start to the school year where every student and faculty member knows exactly where they belong.

acceptable_paraphrases: Start the school year with harmonious scheduling clarity.

traps.note: Mr. Davis requires consecutive double science lab blocks while Dr. Chen requires split single periods across alternate days.
Dr. Chen establishes an explicit teacher welfare constraint forbidding more than three room changes per day.
Mr. Davis notes student council delegates have critical lunch schedule requirements but have not participated.
Rachel suggests automated facial recognition cameras; both stakeholders firmly reject the proposal.

gaps.description: Conflict between consecutive science lab double-periods G3 and alternate-day split periods G4 is unresolved.
Student union council stakeholders are absent despite holding critical preferences regarding lunch period scheduling.

entailment_cases.hypothesis: The school master timetable must prevent assigning multiple classes to the same classroom simultaneously.
All chemistry lab stations must be outfitted with smart RFID beaker sensors connected to an industrial PLC.
Junior instructors may be scheduled to teach in six different classrooms on a single Monday.
All course syllabi must be parsed and indexed using a vector embedding database before class assignment.
